knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 33-year-old male presented with intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, and numbness in both lower limbs for 3 days. Initially managed for partial intestinal obstruction, he awaited diagnostic laparoscopy. The patient developed confusion and systemic hypertension, leading to a transfer to the medical ward. He has no history of diabetes or hypertension. He had been using over-the-counter analgesics for 6 weeks. His medical history includes five similar neurovisceral episodes over 2 years, each requiring acute hospital admissions. The first episode in January 2013 was managed as appendicitis, but symptoms worsened post-surgery, leading to an emergency laparoscopic exploration that revealed no cause. The second episode was managed as sinus tachycardia with beta-blockers. The third episode, associated with fever, was managed conservatively for renal colic. The fourth episode involved transient hyponatremia and elevated serum creatinine, attributed to diclofenac sodium use. knowledge_fragments.content: Majority of our study population presented after 24 hours of symptom onset which is consistent with literatures. Our study showed that the most common symptom at presentation was abdominal pain accounting for 96.6%. Comparable results were seen in many studies in the country, abdominal pain accounting for 100% in a study done in Nekemte and 95.5% in a study done in Debrebirhan. Our study showed that 30% of patients had history of previous intestinal obstruction, which was much higher than a similar study done in Debrebirhan hospital in which only 8% of patients had previous intestinal obstruction.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 20-year-old male arrived at the Emergency Department with complaints of epigastric pain lasting for 6 hours and an episode of vomiting. He had no prior history of abdominal surgery or trauma. Physical examination revealed moderate tenderness in the epigastric region without rebound tenderness or a palpable mass. Bowel sounds were active upon auscultation, and the rectal examination was normal. Upon arrival, his vital signs included a temperature of 37.0°C, blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, and a pulse rate of 85 beats per minute. Laboratory results indicated elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase at 241 IU/l and creatinophosphokinase at 507 IU/l, with no increase in white blood cell count.. Confirmed diagnosis: Intestinal Obstruction Due to an Anomalous Congenital Band. Differential diagnosis includes: Intestinal Obstruction Due to an Anomalous Congenital Band.

knowledge_fragments.content: This study tried to find out the causes, the management outcome and factors that are associated with the management outcome among patients admitted to AURH with the diagnosis of intestinal obstruction within the study period. Though there were many studies about the causes and prevalence of intestinal obstruction in our country, only few studies were conducted on the management outcome and the factors that are associated with it. And to our knowledge there was no study done on intestinal obstruction in our study area.

Other causes of Compound IO found in our study were adhesive intestinal obstruction (n=2) and concomitant sigmoid cancer with small bowel volvulus (n=1). All cases with ISK were found to have gangrenous bowel (either both sigmoid and ileum or only ileum). All in all, 84.6% (n=11) of cases of compound intestinal obstruction were found to have gangrenous intestinal obstruction.

In all ages, intestinal obstruction is manifested by cramping abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Acute

Meckel's diverticulitis is characterized by abdominal pain and tenderness typically localized below or to

the left of the umbilicus; it is often accompanied by vomiting and is similar to appendicitis except for

location of pain.

Children may present with repeated episodes of painless, bright red rectal bleeding, which is usually not

severe enough to cause shock. Adults may also bleed, typically resulting in melena rather than frank

blood.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 21-year-old man presented to the clinic with acute right flank pain, nausea, and vomiting, without constipation or abdominal distention. He had a history of Hirschsprung's disease and had undergone surgery in infancy. He also had a history of prolonged constipation and had been admitted previously due to suspected obstruction but was discharged without complications. On examination, his blood pressure was 125/80, heart rate was 93, respiratory rate was 20, and temperature was 37.8. Physical examination revealed severe costovertebral angle tenderness. Neurologic examination was normal. His history and physical examination were otherwise unremarkable. Urine examination showed microscopic hematuria. Laboratory tests were otherwise unremarkable.. Confirmed diagnosis: Currarino syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Currarino syndrome.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 30-year-old male patient arrived at the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, diarrhea, and vomiting that had persisted for 24 hours. The patient mentioned experiencing a similar episode three months earlier, which was managed conservatively at another facility. His medical history includes posttraumatic stress disorder and chronic cannabis use, consuming 10-15 joints daily. The pain was so intense that the patient was observed by his girlfriend pouring boiling water on himself. Upon admission, the patient exhibited aggressive behavior, posing a risk to himself and others. Blood tests revealed an elevated leucocyte count of 16.88 G/l, while the C-reactive protein level was normal at 0.1 mg/dl. Initial treatment included lorazepam and olanzapine.. Confirmed diagnosis: Multiple intestinal intussusceptions caused by highly impaired gastrointestinal motility. Differential diagnosis includes: Multiple intestinal intussusceptions caused by highly impaired gastrointestinal motility.

She also experienced nausea, vomiting, constipation for 3 days, and a low-grade fever of 38.0°C. Her medical history included ulcerative colitis, for which she was taking azathioprine, mesalazine, and a biological agent; chronic lymphocytic leukemia under monitoring; and hypertension. She had no history of smoking or alcohol use. She was retired and lived with multiple family members. Physical examination of her abdomen indicated signs of peritonitis. Eight years ago, she underwent an abdominal hysterectomy for uterine fibroids. On clinical examination, she was hemodynamically stable. Her abdomen was distended with hyperperistaltic bowel sounds. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed dilated proximal ileal loops with air-fluid levels and collapsed terminal ileal loops. There was an abrupt narrowing and a 'bird beak appearance' in the proximal ileum beneath the anterior abdominal wall. Based on these findings, an emergency laparotomy was planned. During the laparotomy, the proximal ileal loops were found to be grossly dilated, while the terminal ileal loops and large bowel loops were collapsed and appeared unremarkable. The ileal loops were densely adhered to the anterior abdominal wall at the previous scar site, causing luminal obstruction. Extensive adhesiolysis was performed

Interpretation of findings:

Distinguishing pregnancy-related vomiting from vomiting due to other causes

is important. Clinical manifestations help (see

).

Vomiting is less likely to be due to pregnancy if it begins after the 1st trimester or is accompanied by

abdominal pain, diarrhea, or both. Abdominal tenderness may suggest acute abdomen. Meningismus,

neurologic abnormalities, or both suggest a neurologic cause.

Vomiting is more likely to be due to pregnancy if it begins during the 1st trimester, it lasts or recurs over

several days to weeks, abdominal pain is absent, and there are no symptoms or signs involving other

organ systems.

If vomiting appears to be pregnancy-related and is severe (ie, frequent, prolonged, accompanied by

dehydration), hyperemesis gravidarum and hydatidiform mole should be considered.

tree.case_summary:
A 5-year-old female child is brought to a medical office with complaints of progressive abdominal pain that has intensified in the last 24 hours. The father reports a history of constipation, with no bowel movement for the past 72 hours and no bloody stools. She has experienced three episodes of vomiting since the previous night and is refusing food. Her medical and surgical history is unremarkable. Physical examination reveals upper abdominal distention with tympany, but no abdominal mass, involuntary guarding, or rebound tenderness is detected. What is the most probable underlying etiology of her clinical presentation?

Options:
A. Hirschsprung disease
B. Intestinal lymphoma
C. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome
D. Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction
E. Volvulus
F. Malrotation of the gut
G. Pyloric stenosis
H. Intussusception
I. Meckel diverticulum
J. Duodenal web

excluded_candidates: Gastrointestinal obstruction: possible but less likely due to absence of bloody stools and abdominal mass
Inflammatory bowel disease: less likely due to acute presentation and absence of bloody stools
